domain: Develop containerized solutions on Azure
prompt: You deploy a new version of a model-inference API to Azure Container Apps. You must roll the new revision out to 10 percent of traffic, validate its response quality and error rate, then shift all traffic to it, with the ability to instantly roll back. Revisions must be immutable, and no new DNS name or URL should be required. What should you do?
options: Create a second Container App with a new ingress URL and switch DNS when ready.
Redeploy the app in place and monitor error rates before scaling out.
Deploy a new revision of the same Container App and use traffic-splitting (weighted routing) to shift from 10 percent to 100 percent, rolling back by adjusting weights.
Use Azure Front Door to route a fraction of requests to a second app.
explanation: Container Apps revisions are immutable and support weighted traffic splitting between active revisions of the same app on the same ingress, enabling canary rollout and instant rollback by changing weights. A second app plus DNS (option 0) or Front Door (option 3) adds complexity and a new endpoint; an in-place redeploy (option 1) mutates the running revision and prevents instant rollback.

domain: Develop containerized solutions on Azure
prompt: Your GPU model-inference service runs in a container. It must scale the number of replicas based on a custom metric (inference queue depth exposed via Prometheus) and must not require you to manage Kubernetes. Which service and scaling approach should you use?
options: Azure Container Apps with a KEDA scaler bound to the Prometheus metric.
Azure Kubernetes Service with the cluster autoscaler only.
Azure Container Instances with per-second billing.
Azure App Service with CPU percentage autoscale.
explanation: Container Apps supports KEDA scalers, including Prometheus, for scaling on custom metrics without operating Kubernetes. The cluster autoscaler (option 1) scales nodes, not replicas, and requires AKS; ACI (option 2) does not autoscale on custom metrics; App Service (option 3) scales on platform metrics, not custom Prometheus metrics.

docs.label: Set scaling rules in Azure Container Apps

domain: Develop containerized solutions on Azure
prompt: A nightly model-evaluation pipeline runs a container that loads a model, evaluates a dataset, writes results, then exits. The job must be triggered on a schedule, automatically retry on failure up to three times, and terminate after completion so you pay only while it runs. Which service should you use?
options: Azure Kubernetes Service with a Deployment of replicas set to 1.
Azure App Service with an always-on web app.
Azure Container Instances with a restart policy of Always.
Azure Container Apps Jobs with a schedule trigger and a retry policy.
explanation: Container Apps Jobs run containers to completion on a schedule and support configurable retry policies, paying only for execution duration. AKS Deployments and App Service keep the workload running continuously, and ACI with Always restarts rather than terminating after completion.

domain: Develop containerized solutions on Azure
prompt: Your model container takes 90 seconds to download weights and warm up before it can serve requests. Users report 502 errors during scale-out and after each deploy. You must route traffic only to instances that are ready, and allow sufficient warm-up time before the platform marks a replica failed. Which probes should you configure?
options: A single liveness probe with a short timeout.
A startup probe with a generous failure threshold, plus a readiness probe that gates ingress.
Only an HTTP health check on the '/' path of the app.
No probes; rely on the platform default restart policy.
explanation: A startup probe gives slow-starting containers extra time before liveness probing begins, and the readiness probe controls when traffic is routed. A liveness probe alone (option 0) would kill the container during warm-up; the '/' check (option 2) is insufficient; no probes (option 3) cause traffic to reach unready instances.

docs.label: Health probes in Azure Container Apps

domain: Develop containerized solutions on Azure
prompt: Your Container Apps environment must read several API keys and connection strings. You must store them centrally, rotate them without redeploying, and inject them into apps without writing secrets into container images or the Container Apps secret store. Which approach should you use?
options: Store secrets in Azure Key Vault, enable the managed identity on the app, grant it Key Vault data-plane permissions, and resolve secrets through Key Vault references or the Dapr secret store.
Store secrets in the container image's environment variables.
Store secrets in Azure App Configuration as plain values.
Store secrets in a public storage account with SAS tokens.
explanation: Key Vault with a managed identity provides centralized, rotatable secrets resolved at runtime without embedding them in images or the app's own secret store. Options 1 and 3 expose secrets, and option 2 stores plaintext values.

docs.label: Manage secrets in Azure Container Apps

domain: Develop containerized solutions on Azure
prompt: A security requirement states that your Container Apps environment may only send outbound traffic to an allowed set of FQDNs, and all other egress must be denied. You need a central point to filter and inspect outbound traffic. What should you implement?
options: An NSG applied directly to each container replica.
An Azure Front Door endpoint for outbound traffic.
VNet integration for the Container Apps environment with a user-defined route forcing egress through Azure Firewall, using FQDN allow rules.
A Network Security Group on the environment's public IP.
explanation: VNet integration plus a user-defined route through Azure Firewall provides centralized outbound filtering with FQDN rules for the whole environment. NSGs (options 0 and 3) filter by IP, not FQDN, and do not apply as desired to managed environments; Front Door (option 1) is for inbound delivery, not egress filtering.

domain: Develop AI solutions by using Azure data management services
prompt: Your RAG application's retrieval layer must combine keyword (lexical) and vector (semantic) search over the same index, apply semantic ranking to improve relevance, and return citations with each answer. You already call Azure OpenAI. Which service should provide the retrieval index?
options: Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL with a vector index and a separate full-text engine.
Azure AI Search with a hybrid index (BM25 + vector) and semantic ranking.
Azure Cache for Redis with a key-value schema.
Azure Table Storage.
explanation: Azure AI Search provides integrated hybrid retrieval (BM25 + vector) and semantic ranking in a single index designed for RAG grounding and citations. Cosmos DB (option 0) lacks integrated lexical ranking; Redis and Table Storage (options 2 and 3) are not full-text/vector search engines.

domain: Develop AI solutions by using Azure data management services
prompt: Your multi-tenant AI app stores prompt and response records in Cosmos DB for NoSQL. Data has grown such that a single tenant can exceed the 20 GB logical partition limit, causing a single partition to become hot. The most frequent query filters by tenantId and then createdAt. What should you do to scale the tenant's data across multiple physical partitions while keeping that query efficient?
options: Increase the provisioned RU/s of the container.
Choose /id as the partition key.
Switch the container to serverless mode.
Use a hierarchical partition key of /tenantId and a second component such as /createdAt.
explanation: Hierarchical partition keys let you split a tenant across multiple physical partitions (for example, by tenant and a date or ID component) while range queries on the leading key remain efficient. Increasing RU (option 0) does not fix the 20 GB ceiling or hot partition; /id (option 1) breaks tenant queries; serverless (option 2) is a throughput mode, not a partition strategy.

docs.label: Hierarchical partition keys in Azure Cosmos DB

domain: Develop AI solutions by using Azure data management services
prompt: You ground an Azure OpenAI chat model on a large private document corpus using Azure OpenAI on your data. You must improve retrieval quality for long documents by splitting them into smaller units before indexing. Which chunking approach best preserves context and semantic meaning?
options: Split documents into overlapping chunks along natural boundaries (for example, paragraphs or sections) with a small overlap, and index each chunk as a searchable unit.
Index each entire document as a single blob regardless of length.
Truncate every document to 512 characters.
Split documents at fixed 10-character boundaries with no overlap.
explanation: Overlapping chunks on semantic boundaries preserve context and meaning for retrieval. Whole-document indexing (option 1) dilutes relevance; truncation (option 2) loses content; arbitrary fixed splits (option 3) destroy meaning.

docs.label: Use your data with Azure OpenAI

domain: Develop AI solutions by using Azure data management services
prompt: You add pgvector search to Azure Database for PostgreSQL. Queries must return highly accurate nearest neighbors with the lowest query latency, and you can accept a longer index build time and larger memory footprint. Which index type should you choose?
options: A B-tree index on the vector column.
An HNSW index on the vector column.
A GIN index on a scalar column.
No index; rely on sequential scan.
explanation: HNSW provides high recall and fast queries at the cost of build time and memory. IVFFlat is faster to build but trades off recall/latency; B-tree and GIN cannot index vectors for similarity search; a sequential scan (option 3) does not scale.

docs.label: Use pgvector in Azure Database for PostgreSQL

domain: Develop AI solutions by using Azure data management services
prompt: Your AI app calls Azure OpenAI and occasionally exceeds the requests-per-minute limit, returning 429 errors. You must smooth bursts across multiple replicas and enforce a shared per-minute quota with low latency and without changing the model deployment. What should you use?
options: A static in-memory counter per replica.
Azure Front Door rate limiting.
Azure Managed Redis implementing a distributed token-bucket rate limiter keyed by caller.
Azure Service Bus to serialize all model calls.
explanation: A distributed rate limiter in Redis enforces a shared quota across replicas with very low latency. Per-replica counters (option 0) do not share a quota; Front Door (option 1) limits at the edge rather than the model endpoint; Service Bus (option 3) adds serialization and latency, not rate limiting.

domain: Develop AI solutions by using Azure data management services
prompt: You must extract key-value pairs, line items, and totals from scanned invoices in many layouts and languages, and store the structured results in Cosmos DB for downstream processing. You need a prebuilt, low-code Azure AI capability. Which service should you use?
options: Azure AI Vision with image tagging.
Azure AI Speech with speech-to-text.
Azure AI Language with key phrase extraction.
Azure AI Document Intelligence with a prebuilt invoice model.
explanation: Document Intelligence's prebuilt invoice model extracts structured invoice fields such as line items and totals. Vision tags images, Speech transcribes audio, and Language extracts key phrases — none of these extract structured invoice data.

docs.label: What is Azure AI Document Intelligence?

domain: Develop AI solutions by using Azure data management services
prompt: Your app stores short-lived embedding documents that are queried heavily for 30 days and then rarely accessed. You must automatically remove expired documents from the hot container and retain them for a year in cheaper storage for audit, without writing a scheduled cleanup job. What should you do?
options: Set the container TTL to 30 days and accept data loss.
Provision a second container and manually copy old documents nightly.
Use Azure Functions with a timer trigger to delete old documents.
Set a 30-day Time to Live on the container, and use the change feed to capture documents as they expire and archive them to Azure Blob Storage (cool tier).
explanation: TTL automatically deletes expired documents and emits them on the change feed; a change feed consumer archives them to cheaper blob storage before deletion. Option 0 loses data; options 1 and 2 require manual or scheduled logic.

docs.label: Configure time to live in Azure Cosmos DB

domain: Connect to and consume Azure services
prompt: A model-review workflow requires a human to approve or reject generated content. If no approval arrives within 4 hours, the workflow must time out and take a fallback action, and the state must survive process restarts. You want to minimize custom coordination code. What should you use?
options: A Durable Functions orchestration that awaits an external approval event and a durable timer, with a timeout that triggers the fallback.
A Service Bus queue with sessions.
An Event Grid topic with a webhook subscriber.
A single HTTP function with a synchronous long sleep.
explanation: Durable Functions orchestrations support waiting on external events and durable timers with checkpointed state, implementing the human-in-the-loop timeout pattern. The other options do not provide durable, resumable state or timeout semantics without custom code.

domain: Connect to and consume Azure services
prompt: Document chunks for a long report must be embedded and indexed strictly in their original order, and processing must tolerate restarts without reordering. Which Service Bus feature should you use?
options: Topics with SQL filters and no ordering guarantees.
Sessions with session-enabled queues, setting the session ID to the document ID and using session state for ordered, restartable processing.
Multiple subscriptions with fan-out.
Auto-forwarding between queues.
explanation: Service Bus sessions preserve FIFO order within a session and provide session state for checkpointing across restarts. Topics/subscriptions (options 0 and 2) and forwarding (option 3) do not guarantee ordered, resumable processing.

docs.label: Message sessions in Azure Service Bus

domain: Connect to and consume Azure services
prompt: You stream model inference telemetry at high volume and must persist it for later batch analytics while preserving per-device ordering. Multiple independent consumers must read the stream without competing. What should you do?
options: Write to Azure Queue Storage.
Publish to Azure Event Grid.
Send events to Azure Event Hubs using a partition key of device ID, enable Capture to Azure Blob or Data Lake, and use separate consumer groups for each consumer.
Publish to a Service Bus topic.
explanation: Event Hubs provides partition-key ordering, Capture for durable storage, and consumer groups for independent readers at high throughput. Queue Storage (option 0) lacks ordering and consumer groups; Event Grid (option 1) is for discrete routing; Service Bus (option 3) is not designed for this ingestion scale.

domain: Connect to and consume Azure services
prompt: Your Azure Functions app must be always-warm to avoid cold starts for a latency-sensitive AI API, connect to resources over a private virtual network, and scale elastically. Which hosting plan should you choose?
options: Consumption plan.
Flex Consumption plan with no VNet.
Dedicated (App Service) plan with a fixed instance count.
Premium plan with pre-warmed instances and VNet integration.
explanation: The Premium plan provides pre-warmed (always-ready) instances to avoid cold starts, elastic scaling, and VNet integration. Consumption (option 0) has cold starts and no VNet; Flex Consumption (option 1) is not private-network; Dedicated (option 2) does not scale elastically.

domain: Connect to and consume Azure services
prompt: Your chat API must begin returning tokens to the user as soon as they are generated to minimize perceived latency, using the Azure OpenAI SDK. Which approach should you implement?
options: Use streaming completions and flush response tokens incrementally to the client as they arrive.
Wait for the full completion, then return the entire payload at once.
Poll the completion with a timer every 5 seconds.
Buffer all tokens and return a single JSON document.
explanation: Streaming returns tokens as they are generated, reducing time-to-first-token. Waiting for the full response (options 1 and 3) and polling (option 2) add avoidable latency.

domain: Connect to and consume Azure services
prompt: A batch inference orchestration must fan out work to many workers, aggregate results, and resume from the last completed step if a worker fails mid-run, without duplicating completed work. Which pattern should you use?
options: Multiple HTTP functions coordinated by a Cosmos DB state table you write yourself.
A Service Bus topic with competing consumers.
A Durable Functions orchestration with fan-out/fan-in, relying on checkpointed orchestration state and idempotent activities.
A single long-running HTTP request that blocks until all workers finish.
explanation: Durable Functions orchestrations checkpoint progress and can replay, resuming after failures; fan-out/fan-in aggregates parallel work. Options 0 and 1 require hand-written coordination; option 3 is not resilient to failures or restarts.

domain: Secure, monitor, and troubleshoot Azure solutions
prompt: Two microservices need different levels of access: one reads and writes a storage account and calls Azure OpenAI, the other only reads a Cosmos DB container. You must avoid shared credentials and apply least privilege per service. Which identity strategy should you use?
options: One system-assigned managed identity shared by both services with Contributor on the subscription.
A separate user-assigned managed identity per service, each granted only the specific roles it needs, scoped to the specific resources.
A single service principal with a client secret stored in each service.
Storage account keys and Cosmos DB keys embedded in configuration.
explanation: Separate user-assigned managed identities enable per-service, scoped least-privilege roles with no shared secrets. A shared Contributor identity (option 0) over-provisions; client secrets and embedded keys (options 2 and 3) are shared and insecure.

domain: Secure, monitor, and troubleshoot Azure solutions
prompt: Your high-traffic AI app sends a very large volume of telemetry to Application Insights, and ingestion cost is too high. You must retain all failures and errors but reduce the volume of successful request telemetry. What should you configure?
options: Adaptive sampling in Application Insights, which reduces the volume of high-frequency successful calls while retaining exceptions and failures.
Disable Application Insights entirely.
Increase the ingestion sampling rate to 100 percent for all telemetry.
Delete telemetry after one day.
explanation: Adaptive sampling automatically limits the volume of typical (successful) telemetry while keeping failures and exceptions, controlling cost. Disabling (option 1) loses visibility; 100 percent sampling (option 2) captures everything at full cost; short retention (option 3) does not reduce ingestion cost.

domain: Secure, monitor, and troubleshoot Azure solutions
prompt: You must keep application logs queryable in Log Analytics for 30 days and additionally preserve them for 7 years for regulatory audit at the lowest cost, without keeping them hot. What should you configure?
options: Set Log Analytics retention to 7 years.
Export logs to a CSV in source control.
Store logs only in Application Insights for 30 days.
Set Log Analytics interactive retention to 30 days and configure the archive tier (or export to Azure Storage) for long-term retention.
explanation: Separating interactive retention from cheaper long-term archive or export minimizes cost while meeting both requirements. Keeping everything hot for 7 years (option 0) is expensive; a CSV in source control (option 1) is not an audit solution; 30-day-only retention (option 2) fails the 7-year requirement.

docs.label: Data retention and archive in Azure Monitor Logs

domain: Secure, monitor, and troubleshoot Azure solutions
prompt: You need to list all failed requests and, for each, the corresponding exception message, to correlate errors in your AI API. Which KQL query should you use?
options: requests | where success == false | count
requests | where success == false | join kind=inner (exceptions) on operation_Id | project timestamp, operation_Id, name, message
exceptions | where timestamp > ago(1d) | take 50
requests | summarize count() by resultCode
explanation: Joining failed requests to exceptions on operation_Id correlates each failure with its exception message. Option 0 counts only; option 2 lists exceptions in isolation; option 3 aggregates counts without error correlation.

domain: Secure, monitor, and troubleshoot Azure solutions
prompt: You must ensure a deleted Key Vault secret or key can be recovered for 90 days and that a malicious actor cannot permanently delete the vault (and its keys) before recovery. Which two features should you enable?
options: Enable purge protection only.
Enable soft-delete only.
Enable soft-delete (90-day retention) together with purge protection.
Back up the vault to Azure Files weekly.
explanation: Soft-delete allows recovery for a retention period, and purge protection prevents forced permanent deletion during that window. Soft-delete alone (option 1) still permits purging; purge protection alone (option 0) is incomplete; file backups (option 3) do not protect key material.

domain: Secure, monitor, and troubleshoot Azure solutions
prompt: A new revision of your Container App fails to start, and traffic never rolls over to it. You need to determine why the revision is stuck and see container startup logs and exit codes. What should you do?
options: Inspect the revision status and use the Container Apps system logs (Azure Monitor / Log Analytics) to view container startup logs, events, and exit codes for that revision.
Look only at Azure Activity Log for control-plane events.
Restart the environment and assume it will recover.
Delete the container registry image.
explanation: Container Apps exposes revision status and system logs in Azure Monitor/Log Analytics showing startup failures, events, and exit codes. Activity Log (option 1) shows only management-plane operations; restarting (option 2) or deleting the image (option 3) does not diagnose the failure.
